<reason>B won by reframing the comparison that the motion actually requires: four-day weeks are adopted by under-resourced rural districts whose realistic alternative is an understaffed five-day week, and A never dislodged that baseline. A's central "money or hours, not both" trap was internally inconsistent with A's own opening (savings come from buses, food, utilities, not teacher hours) and B exposed this cleanly; A effectively conceded in A4.1 that the lines do shrink and retreated to "it's small," which B then reframed as decisive in a district whose deficit is that same one or two percent. A's best surviving material — the near-zero ceiling, retention invisible in achievement, and desperate districts compressing hours — was real pressure, but B answered each adequately (mixed averages, unoffered courses not on the test, statutory hour minimums, teachers trading pay for schedule), while A's "same vacancy either way" answer to B's pointed Q2 was asserted rather than argued. Given the motion's burden that harm must exceed help, B's "near zero does not outweigh anything" is the cleaner decision rule. A was polished and disciplined but spent its late speeches defending a collapsing mechanism rather than the baseline.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B2.1–B2.3 dismantling A's "trap": instructional hours are preserved by lengthening four days, savings come from separate fifth-day budget lines A itself named, and retention depends on the flexible weekday rather than shortened hours — forcing A's concession in A4.1 that the savings exist and shifting the debate to B's terrain.</best_rebuttal>
